paras: The Charlieville shooting was the shooting of an unnamed Black man at Charlieville, Louisiana, on a Monday in late August 1881. He was reported to be mortally wounded, and the men who shot him were said to be still at large. The Richland Beacon, whose short item was reprinted by other Louisiana papers, treated it as the latest in a run of such shootings and demanded arrests.

The only account came to the Richland Beacon from the mail carrier, who reported that "another colored man was shot, and it was thought mortally wounded, at Charlieville" the previous Monday. The item did not name the victim, the place where he was shot, the time of day, the number of attackers or any reason for the attack. Its word "another" points to earlier shootings of Black men in the area, but these were not described.

At the time of the report no one had been arrested, and the Beacon described the "murderers" as "now at large." No later report of the victim's death or recovery, an inquest, an arrest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached readers only as a two-sentence exchange item credited to the Richland Beacon. The Morehouse Clarion ran it on 2 September 1881 in its "State Items" column, and the Louisiana Capitolian of Baton Rouge printed nearly the same words the next day among other parish news. In the Beacon's words, "There is no telling where this murdering business will end, if the murderers now at large are not arrested and brought to justice."

Neither reprinting paper added comment of its own, and both set the item beside unrelated crop and town news. The same exchange columns also carried a Beacon story of a Black man accused of stealing a cow being sewn inside the animal's carcass in Morehouse parish, which the Beacon presented as "a new and original mode of punishing a cow thief."
